title: Burgundy History & Cultural Heritage In-Depth Study
description: Tracing 2,000 years of Burgundy wine civilisation from Roman times through the Middle Ages, the Valois Dukes, the Revolution, phylloxera, the AOC system, and modern cultural influence

lessons.0.slides.0.description: Exploring the origins and early development of Burgundy wine
lessons.0.slides.1.title: The Roman Wine Legacy (1st–5th centuries)
lessons.0.slides.1.content: In 52 BC, following Caesar's conquest of Gaul, the Romans established viticulture in the Burgundy region (then the territory of the Aedui tribe). Archaeological evidence reveals systematic vineyard planning around Autun, Beaune, and Dijon. The Romans introduced Mediterranean grape varieties and winemaking techniques, and established a complete system from cultivation to storage.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🏛️ Key Roman Contributions
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Established hillside planting systems — discovered the advantage of south-east-facing slopes
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Via Agrippa trade route — linking the Mediterranean to Northern Europe
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Established Autun as a wine trade centre
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Records of Burgundy wine in the poetry of Roman poet Ausonius
lessons.0.slides.3.title: The Monastic Golden Age (6th–15th centuries)
lessons.0.slides.3.content: The medieval monastic system utterly transformed the fate of Burgundy wine. Cistercian and Benedictine monks regarded viticulture as sacred work; they had the time, knowledge, and motivation to study each plot of land in depth. The Abbey of Cîteaux (founded 1098) and the Abbey of Cluny became centres of wine knowledge.
lessons.0.slides.4.title: ⛪ The Revolutionary Monastic Contributions
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 1336 — completion of the walls of Clos de Vougeot
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: Developed the 'Climat' system — precise parcel demarcation
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: Varietal selection — identifying the most suitable grape varieties
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: Winemaking — recording the distinctive character of different parcels
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: Established a quality hierarchy — the early concept of Grand Cru
lessons.0.slides.4.points.5: Manuscript records — detailed vineyard management notes
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 💡 Cultural Insight
lessons.0.slides.5.content: While working in the vineyards each day, the monks would taste the soil to understand the mineral character of each plot. This tradition of 'tasting the earth' (goûter la terre) remains an important practice for Burgundy winemakers to this day. The monks believed that understanding the flavour of the land was the path to understanding the soul of the wine.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: 📜 A Millennium of Burgundy Wine: From the Roman Empire to UNESCO World Heritage
lessons.0.slides.6.content: 2,000 years of evolution: Roman conquest introduces viticulture → Monastic golden age → Valois Dukes' quality revolution → French Revolution fragmenting ownership → Phylloxera crisis and reconstruction → Establishment of the AOC system → Modern global recognition.

lessons.1.title: The Valois Dukes and the Golden Age of Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.0.title: The Valois Dukes and the Golden Age of Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 16 min
lessons.1.slides.0.description: The political and cultural zenith of Burgundy wine in the 14th and 15th centuries
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Philip the Bold and the Quality Revolution (1363–1404)
lessons.1.slides.1.content: In 1395, Duke Philip II of Burgundy (Philippe le Hardi) issued one of the most important decrees in wine history: a ban on planting Gamay, requiring all vines to be replaced with Pinot Noir. He described Gamay as a 'very bad and disloyal plant' (très mauvais et très déloyal plant). This decision laid the quality foundation of Burgundy wine and established the regional boundary between present-day Burgundy (Pinot Noir) and Beaujolais (Gamay).
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 👑 The Valois Dukes' Wine Policies
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: 1416 — prohibition of fertilisation to improve quality
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Establishment of appellation boundaries and quality controls
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Promotion of Burgundy wine as a diplomatic gift
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Hospices de Beaune (charitable hospital) founded in 1443
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Wine became the economic pillar of the Duchy
lessons.1.slides.3.title: A Luxury Good for the European Court
lessons.1.slides.3.content: By the 15th century Burgundy wine had become one of the most expensive commodities in Europe. The ducal court at Dijon was among the most opulent in Europe, and wine was a vital tool of diplomatic negotiation. Pope Clement VI famously declared: 'A banquet without Burgundy wine does not deserve the name.'

lessons.2.title: The French Revolution and the Property Revolution
lessons.2.slides.0.title: The French Revolution and the Property Revolution
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 14 min
lessons.2.slides.0.description: How 1789 shaped the modern structure of the Burgundy wine industry
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Seizure and Auction of Church Lands
lessons.2.slides.1.content: After the French Revolution of 1789, the National Assembly confiscated the lands of the Church and aristocracy, including Burgundy's finest vineyards. These vineyards were broken into small parcels and sold at auction to the middle classes and peasants, permanently transforming Burgundy's ownership structure. Monastic estates that had once formed a single vast vineyard (such as Clos de Vougeot) were divided among dozens of owners.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: ⚖️ The Far-Reaching Impact of the Revolution
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Large vineyards were fragmented — Clos de Vougeot went from one owner to 80+
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Created a 'smallholder culture' — average holding just 2–3 hectares
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Napoleonic Code of Inheritance — land must be divided equally among all children
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Perpetual fragmentation — each inheritance divides the land again
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: Gave birth to the Négociant system — needed to aggregate smallholder produce
lessons.2.slides.3.title: The Legacy of the Napoleonic Code
lessons.2.slides.3.content: The Napoleonic Code of 1804 required property to be divided equally among all heirs, leading to continuous vineyard fragmentation. Today, many Grand Crus are split among dozens or even hundreds of owners. Échézeaux has 84 owners, Clos de Vougeot has 80 owners — the smallest parcel may consist of just a few rows of vines.
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Ownership Structure — A Comparison
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🔑 Key Concept: The Birth of the Négociant System
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: Négociant — purchases grapes or wine from small growers
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: Négociant-Éleveur — responsible for elevage and blending
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: Builds brands and distribution — individual smallholders cannot sell directly
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: Quality assurance role — selects and blends across different parcels
lessons.2.slides.5.points.4: Famous négociants: Bouchard Père & Fils (1731), Joseph Drouhin (1880)

lessons.3.title: The Phylloxera Crisis and Reconstruction
lessons.3.slides.0.title: The Phylloxera Crisis and Reconstruction
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 min
lessons.3.slides.0.description: The late-19th-century vineyard catastrophe and rebirth
lessons.3.slides.1.title: The Phylloxera Invasion (1863–1890s)
lessons.3.slides.1.content: In 1863, the deadly phylloxera louse arrived in France from America. This minute insect attacked vine roots and by the 1880s had destroyed most of France's vineyards. Between 1878 and 1895, Burgundy lost more than 80 % of its vineyards. Many ancient old vines were lost entirely, and the whole industry faced annihilation.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🐛 Crisis Timeline
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Early 1890s — grafting solution begins to spread
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: 1900s — reconstruction essentially complete, but landscape transformed
lessons.3.slides.3.title: The Solution: American Rootstock Grafting
lessons.3.slides.3.content: The ultimate solution was to graft European Vitis vinifera (wine grape) vines onto phylloxera-resistant American rootstocks. This required replanting every vineyard and sparked an ongoing debate about 'authenticity'. Burgundy producers insisted on using the most neutral rootstocks available (such as SO4, 41B) to minimise any impact on terroir expression.
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🔬 Grafting Technique and Rootstock Selection
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: Selection principle: minimise vigour, respect terroir
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: Debate: flavour differences between pre- and post-grafting vines
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: Exceptions: Chile and certain Greek islands still have own-rooted vines
lessons.3.slides.4.points.4: Today: virtually all Burgundy vines are grafted
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Post-Crisis Industry Restructuring
lessons.3.slides.5.content: The reconstruction process led to the bankruptcy of many smallholders, with much of their land acquired by négociants, reinforcing the Négociant system. At the same time, replanting offered an opportunity to reconsider varieties, planting density, and management methods. Inferior parcels were abandoned, and a consensus emerged around focusing on the best terroirs.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 📊 Long-Term Impact
lessons.3.slides.6.points.0: Completely eliminated the pre-phylloxera vine stock
lessons.3.slides.6.points.1: Accelerated the trend of négociants acquiring land
lessons.3.slides.6.points.2: Promoted a more scientific approach to viticulture
lessons.3.slides.6.points.3: Strengthened the pursuit of terroir precision
lessons.3.slides.6.points.4: Stimulated modern wine chemistry and microbiology research
lessons.3.slides.6.points.5: The philosophical debate on 'authenticity' continues to this day

lessons.4.slides.0.title: Establishing the AOC System and Appellation Definitions
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 16 min
lessons.4.slides.0.description: The quality revolution and controlled-appellation system of the early 20th century
lessons.4.slides.1.title: The Fraud Crisis and the Need for Legal Protection
lessons.4.slides.1.content: In the early 20th century, counterfeit Burgundy wine was rampant, severely damaging the region's reputation. The 1905 wine-fraud scandal revealed that 80 % of wine labelled 'Burgundy' on the market did not come from Burgundy at all. This spurred producers to unite and demand legal protection. Bordeaux and Champagne faced similar problems at the same time, jointly pushing for appellations-of-origin legislation.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: ⚖️ The History of the AOC System
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: 1905 — first law protecting appellations of origin
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: 1935 — INAO (Institut National des Appellations d'Origine) established
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: 1937 — detailed demarcation of Grand Cru and Premier Cru boundaries
lessons.4.slides.3.title: Burgundy's Pyramid Classification System
lessons.4.slides.3.content: Burgundy's AOC system is the world's most complex and refined, reflecting a millennium of terroir observation. The system has four levels: Régionale (Bourgogne), Village, Premier Cru, and Grand Cru. This system is based not on domaine brands but on the quality potential of the land itself.
lessons.4.slides.4.title: 🏆 Burgundy AOC Four-Level Pyramid — Production Distribution
lessons.4.slides.4.content: Grand Cru represents just 1 % of production but commands the highest prices; Régionale accounts for 53 % and is the most accessible. The higher up the pyramid, the scarcer the wine and the higher the price — a perfect illustration of 'scarcity = value'.
lessons.4.slides.5.title: 🏆 The Four-Level Pyramid Explained
lessons.4.slides.5.points.0: Grand Cru — 33 appellations, 1 % of production, highest quality potential
lessons.4.slides.5.points.1: Premier Cru — 640 appellations, 10 % of production, outstanding parcels
lessons.4.slides.6.title: Burgundy vs Bordeaux Classification — Compared
lessons.4.slides.7.title: The Climat System — UNESCO World Heritage
lessons.4.slides.7.content: On 4 July 2015, Burgundy's Climat system (1,247 named parcels) was inscribed on the UNESCO World Cultural Heritage list — the first wine region in the world to receive this honour for its vineyard cultural landscape. UNESCO recognised it as 'an exemplar of millennia of human interaction with the natural environment, and a cultural achievement of precise land demarcation and nomenclature'.

lessons.5.slides.0.description: The special place of Burgundy in contemporary wine culture
lessons.5.slides.1.title: The Burgundy Phenomenon
lessons.5.slides.1.content: In the 21st century Burgundy wine has transcended the category of beverage to become a cultural symbol. The 2013 documentary SOMM and the 2016 film 'Romanée-Conti: The World's Most Expensive Wine' brought Burgundy to a mass audience. In Asia — particularly Hong Kong, Japan, and mainland China — Burgundy wine has become an emblem of taste and status.

lessons.5.slides.2.points.0: DRC (Domaine de la Romanée-Conti) — average price above $10,000 per bottle
lessons.5.slides.2.points.1: Top restaurant wine lists — Burgundy's share continues to rise

lessons.5.slides.2.points.3: Social media — the #Burgundy hashtag reaching tens of millions
lessons.5.slides.2.points.4: Wine pilgrimage — the Côte d'Or is a must-visit destination for enthusiasts
lessons.5.slides.3.title: Climate Change and the Organic Movement
lessons.5.slides.3.content: Burgundy faces the challenge of climate change: earlier harvests, rising alcohol, falling acidity. At the same time, biodynamic viticulture and organic farming are advancing rapidly. Top domaines such as Domaine Leroy and Domaine de la Romanée-Conti are leading the way in organic and biodynamic certification. By 2020, certified organic vineyard area in Burgundy had reached 15 %, with a target of 50 % by 2030.

lessons.5.slides.5.title: Traditional vs Modern Orientation
lessons.5.slides.6.title: 💡 Burgundy's Philosophical Legacy
lessons.5.slides.6.content: The heart of Burgundy wine culture is 'humility' — winemakers see themselves as interpreters of the terroir, not its creators. This philosophy has influenced the global fine-wine movement. From Oregon to New Zealand, from Sonoma to Germany, the finest winemakers all aspire to 'respect the terroir the way Burgundy does'. Burgundy has demonstrated that the greatest wines come from a deep understanding and reverence for the land.
